messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Delivery Driver
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arthur sat in the waiting room of the clinic, seventy-seven years old, his hands resting on a familiar leather delivery bag. The assault that had altered his days had occurred a few years prior, during a routine evening drop-off on his assigned route. He had been unloading a heavy crate when a customer, unsteady from a long shift, had stumbled backward and driven a heavy work boot into Arthur’s chest. The man had then kicked the van’s side door in frustration. The sharp, sudden clang had echoed through the alley, and Arthur had stood frozen, his back pressed against the cold brick wall, feeling the ground tilt beneath him. The violence had been close, unexpected, and entirely unannounced. In the weeks that followed, Arthur found himself constantly bracing. What frightened him most was the unpredictability of his own route. He was certain that a man could turn on him in any aisle, that the world had grown sharp at the edges. His beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed. He used to think that a steady route and careful attention kept danger at bay, but now he felt exposed to random force. He began to doubt himself as well. When he packed the van each morning, he would pause at the back door, wondering if he had latched it correctly, if he had loaded the heavy crates the right way. He could not trust that he will do the right thing. Arthur worked hard at keeping busy with other things. He volunteered for extra stops, organized his tool kit down to the last wrench, and spent his breaks wiping down the steering wheel. At the same time, he suppressed thoughts about the trauma. He would hum old radio tunes, watch the passing scenery, and deliberately push the memory of the heavy boot and the brick wall to the edges of his mind. He was certain that if he thought about the event, he will not be able to handle it, so he kept the door to that memory firmly closed. When the quiet grew too loud, he overated. He would eat excessively, finishing a second slice of toast or a full bag of peanuts not out of hunger but to manage the distress building in his chest. These habits settled into his days without replacing one another; they simply co-existed, filling the space he had once filled with easy certainty. The habits took root in the specifics of his daily environment. At the market, he navigated the narrow grocery aisles with his shoulders squared, avoiding eye contact with other men who moved too quickly. In his own home, his wife, Eleanor, noticed how he filled the silence with the scrape of cutlery and the turn of pages. He declined evening walks when the streetlights flickered on, and he started taking his lunch earlier so he could avoid the crowded afternoons. The consequences of these choices accumulated over months. His refusal of the later routes meant a steady drop in his weekly pay, and he began to carry the weight of it silently. At home, Eleanor noticed how he avoided the back seats of cars, how he measured his steps on the porch, as though each movement might trigger another fall. He worked hard at keeping busy, yet the busyness often felt like a careful balancing act rather than a natural rhythm. It was the morning he almost missed a scheduled stop because he was staring at the van’s side mirror, watching his own reflection, that Arthur finally decided to seek help. He had come to believe that the quiet life he was building was no longer enough to hold the fear at bay. What he hoped for most was a way to step outside without bracing for impact, a return to the predictable map he had once known. He sat in the therapist’s office now, hands resting on his knees, and spoke about the heavy boot, the brick wall, and the sudden clang that still echoed in his mind when the wind caught the alley doors. He was certain the world had changed, but he was ready to learn how to walk through it again.
